narrative:
The model estimates you have a 14% chance of failing your final year. While this is not a high probability, it is enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction that you might fail is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. Surprisingly, this actually pushes the model toward expecting you to fail. Among students who passed, having zero previous failures is the norm, but in your specific combination of circumstances the model sees the complete lack of any prior academic struggle as a warning sign rather than a guarantee of success.

The second strongest influence is the quality of your family relationships, which you described as good. This works in your favor and pulls the prediction toward passing. However, its positive effect is not strong enough to outweigh the other signals.

Third, your reason for choosing this school—its reputation—also nudges the outcome slightly toward passing compared with students who chose it for other reasons.

To improve, focus on building consistent study habits now, even though you have no history of failure. Since almost all students who succeed want to continue into higher education just as you do, use that motivation. Consider increasing your weekly study time beyond the 2–5 hours you currently spend, and talk with your mother and father, both of whom have higher education, about creating a structured plan to turn your 14% risk into a clear pass. Taking the remedial courses seriously will help close any small gaps before they grow.
